title: Movie Ticket Booking
scopeHtml: Scope: atomic multi-seat hold with TTL, confirm after payment, lazy expiry with an injected clock, double-booking races, DB and Redis locking, ticket-drop load.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a movie ticket booking system (BookMyShow style): browse shows, pick seats, hold them while paying, confirm the booking, and never sell one seat twice.

Clarify: one theatre or many? Seat map per show? How long is a hold (typically 5 to 10 minutes)? Can a user book several seats at once (yes, all-or-nothing)? Payment is external and can fail or time out. Pricing tiers and cancellation are follow-ups. (Here: shows with a seat grid, atomic multi-seat hold with TTL, confirm after payment, release on failure.)

Worked example. A show has 50 seats (5 rows x 10). Alice holds A1,A2 at 10:00 with a 5-minute TTL (expiry 10:05). Bob tries A2,A3 at 10:01: A2 is locked so he gets nothing, and A3 must stay free (atomicity). Bob retries for A3 only and gets it. Alice pays at 10:03 and A1,A2 become BOOKED. On Friday night with 3,000 users on one blockbuster show, many will click the same "best seats" at the same second; exactly one may win each.

Industry examples. BookMyShow, PVR, Ticketmaster (the hold-then-pay flow, with a visible countdown), airline seat selection, IRCTC Tatkal. Ticketmaster adds a virtual waiting room to cap concurrency before the seat map.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant host puts a "reserved" card on a table while you finish ordering; if you do not sit down in 5 minutes the card is removed.

Common interview traps.

  • Check-then-act without a lock: "if seat is free, then book" lets two users both pass the check.
  • Forgetting that payment takes time, so you need a temporary hold, not an immediate booking.
  • Holding seats forever if the user closes the tab (needs expiry).

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Show: the screening (movie, screen, time, price). Owns its seat states. This is the unit of locking.
  • SeatState: AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED.
  • Lock info per seat: owner userId and expiry time.
  • Booking: id, show, user, seats, amount. Created only on confirm.
  • BookingService: API: hold, pay (confirm), cancelHold.
  • (Out of scope here: Movie, Theatre, Screen, Payment, User catalog. They are plain data.)

Decision gravity. Making Show the consistency boundary (all seats of one show behind one lock) is simple and correct, and it is reversible: if a show's lock gets hot, move to per-seat locks. Booking stays a separate object created only after payment, so there are no half-bookings to clean up.

Everyday analogy. Each show is a seating chart on a clipboard; whoever holds the clipboard edits it, one person at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Modelling the lock as a separate global table without tying it to the show, so it is hard to make atomic.
  • Allowing BOOKED to go back to AVAILABLE without a cancellation flow.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
| BookingService            |--many--->| Show                      |
| shows: Map<id, Show>      |          | id, pricePerSeat          |
| hold(show,user,seats)     |          | state: Map<seat,State>    |
| pay(show,user,seats)      |          | lockOwner: Map<seat,user> |
| cancelHold(...)           |          | lockExpiry: Map<seat,ms>  |
+---------------------------+          | clock: LongSupplier       |
                                       | lockSeats(user,seats)     |
 <<enum>> SeatState                    | confirm(id,user,seats)    |
 AVAILABLE | LOCKED | BOOKED          | release(user,seats)       |
                                       +---------------------------+
+---------------------------+                      |
| Booking                   |<---------creates-----+
| id, showId, userId        |
| seats, amount             |
+---------------------------+

How to read it. The clock is injected, so tests can move time forward instead of sleeping 5 minutes. All state-changing methods on Show are synchronized, so each is atomic.

Common interview traps.

  • Using System.currentTimeMillis() directly; expiry becomes untestable.
  • Exposing the seat map as a mutable collection.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Pessimistic lock per show (synchronized): Why: the invariant "no seat is sold twice" spans several seats, so one critical section is the simplest way to be correct. Alternative: optimistic version number on the show/seat row and retry on conflict (better when conflicts are rare). Breaks when: one show is so hot that a single lock is the bottleneck. Reversible.
  • Two-phase reservation (hold, then confirm): a classic way to handle slow external steps. The hold is a lease with a TTL, not a permanent claim.
  • Lazy expiry: a lock past its expiry is treated as AVAILABLE the next time anyone looks (expireIfStale). Correctness does not depend on a cleanup thread; a background sweeper is only an optimisation for UI refresh. Why: fewer moving parts, no race between the sweeper and a payment.
  • All-or-nothing: validate every requested seat first, then mutate. No rollback code needed because nothing was changed before validation passed.
  • Strategy (follow-up): pricing (weekday, weekend, premium rows).

Industry examples. Redis SET key value NX PX 300000 is the standard distributed seat-lock primitive (set if absent with a 5-minute expiry); DynamoDB conditional writes or SQL UPDATE seats SET status='LOCKED' WHERE id=? AND status='AVAILABLE' do the same atomically (check rows affected).

Everyday analogy. A library "hold" slip on a book: valid for 3 days, then it goes back to the shelf automatically.

Common interview traps.

  • Confirm without re-validating the lock: payment succeeds at minute 6 after the lock expired and someone else got the seat. Confirm must check "still locked by me".
  • Releasing someone else's lock in cancelHold; check the owner.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (show, atomic lock, confirm, service, test with a 100-thread race):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

enum SeatState { AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED }

class Booking {
    final String id, showId, userId; final List<String> seats; final long amount;
    Booking(String id, String showId, String userId, List<String> seats, long amount) {
        this.id = id; this.showId = showId; this.userId = userId; this.seats = seats; this.amount = amount;
    }
}

/** One screening. ALL seat state for the show lives behind this object's lock, so a multi-seat hold is atomic. */
class Show {
    final String id; final long pricePerSeat;
    private final Map<String, SeatState> state = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, String> lockOwner = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Long> lockExpiry = new HashMap<>();
    private final LongSupplier clock; private final long lockTtlMs;

    Show(String id, int rows, int cols, long pricePerSeat, LongSupplier clock, long lockTtlMs) {
        this.id = id; this.pricePerSeat = pricePerSeat; this.clock = clock; this.lockTtlMs = lockTtlMs;
        for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++) for (int c = 1; c <= cols; c++) state.put("" + (char) ('A' + r) + c, SeatState.AVAILABLE);
    }

    /** All-or-nothing: either every requested seat is held for this user, or none is. */
    synchronized boolean lockSeats(String userId, List<String> seats) {
        for (String s : seats) {
            if (!state.containsKey(s)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no seat " + s);
            expireIfStale(s);
            if (state.get(s) != SeatState.AVAILABLE) return false;
        }
        long exp = clock.getAsLong() + lockTtlMs;
        for (String s : seats) { state.put(s, SeatState.LOCKED); lockOwner.put(s, userId); lockExpiry.put(s, exp); }
        return true;
    }

    /** Payment succeeded: lock must still be ours and unexpired, else the seat may already be someone else's. */
    synchronized Booking confirm(String bookingId, String userId, List<String> seats) {
        for (String s : seats) {
            expireIfStale(s);
            if (state.get(s) != SeatState.LOCKED || !userId.equals(lockOwner.get(s)))
                throw new IllegalStateException("lock lost for " + s);
        }
        for (String s : seats) { state.put(s, SeatState.BOOKED); lockOwner.remove(s); lockExpiry.remove(s); }
        return new Booking(bookingId, id, userId, seats, pricePerSeat * seats.size());
    }

    synchronized void release(String userId, List<String> seats) {
        for (String s : seats)
            if (state.get(s) == SeatState.LOCKED && userId.equals(lockOwner.get(s))) free(s);
    }

    synchronized SeatState stateOf(String seat) { expireIfStale(seat); return state.get(seat); }

    private void expireIfStale(String s) {            // lazy expiry: no background thread needed for correctness
        if (state.get(s) == SeatState.LOCKED && clock.getAsLong() >= lockExpiry.get(s)) free(s);
    }
    private void free(String s) { state.put(s, SeatState.AVAILABLE); lockOwner.remove(s); lockExpiry.remove(s); }
}

class BookingService {
    private final Map<String, Show> shows = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicInteger ids = new AtomicInteger();
    void addShow(Show s) { shows.put(s.id, s); }
    boolean hold(String showId, String userId, List<String> seats) { return shows.get(showId).lockSeats(userId, seats); }
    Booking pay(String showId, String userId, List<String> seats) {
        return shows.get(showId).confirm("BK" + ids.incrementAndGet(), userId, seats);   // payment gateway call would go before this
    }
    void cancelHold(String showId, String userId, List<String> seats) { shows.get(showId).release(userId, seats); }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        long[] now = {0};                                   // fake clock
        BookingService svc = new BookingService();
        svc.addShow(new Show("S1", 5, 10, 250, () -> now[0], 5 * 60_000));

        check(svc.hold("S1", "alice", List.of("A1", "A2")), "alice holds");
        check(!svc.hold("S1", "bob", List.of("A2", "A3")), "bob blocked, and A3 must stay free (atomic)");
        check(svc.hold("S1", "bob", List.of("A3")), "A3 was not leaked by the failed attempt");
        Booking b = svc.pay("S1", "alice", List.of("A1", "A2"));
        check(b.amount == 500, "price");

        svc.hold("S1", "bob", List.of("B1"));
        now[0] += 5 * 60_000;                               // lock expires
        check(svc.hold("S1", "carol", List.of("B1")), "carol takes expired seat");
        boolean lost = false;
        try { svc.pay("S1", "bob", List.of("B1")); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { lost = true; }
        check(lost, "bob's late payment rejected");

        // race: 100 users fight for the same seat, exactly one wins
        AtomicInteger winners = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(100);
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            final String u = "u" + i;
            pool.submit(() -> {
                try { go.await(); if (svc.hold("S1", u, List.of("E5"))) winners.incrementAndGet(); }
                catch (InterruptedException ignored) {} finally { done.countDown(); }
            });
        }
        go.countDown(); done.await(); pool.shutdown();
        check(winners.get() == 1, "exactly one winner, got " + winners.get());
        System.out.println("P10 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

enum class SeatState { AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED }

class Show(val id: String, rows: Int, cols: Int, val price: Long,
           private val clock: () -> Long, private val ttlMs: Long) {
    private val state = LinkedHashMap<String, SeatState>()
    private val owner = HashMap<String, String>()
    private val expiry = HashMap<String, Long>()

    init { for (r in 0 until rows) for (c in 1..cols) state["${'A' + r}$c"] = SeatState.AVAILABLE }

    @Synchronized fun lockSeats(user: String, seats: List<String>): Boolean {
        seats.forEach { require(it in state) { "no seat $it" }; expireIfStale(it) }
        if (seats.any { state[it] != SeatState.AVAILABLE }) return false
        val exp = clock() + ttlMs
        seats.forEach { state[it] = SeatState.LOCKED; owner[it] = user; expiry[it] = exp }
        return true
    }

    @Synchronized fun confirm(user: String, seats: List<String>): Long {
        seats.forEach { expireIfStale(it) }
        check(seats.all { state[it] == SeatState.LOCKED && owner[it] == user }) { "lock lost" }
        seats.forEach { state[it] = SeatState.BOOKED; owner.remove(it); expiry.remove(it) }
        return price * seats.size
    }

    private fun expireIfStale(s: String) {
        if (state[s] == SeatState.LOCKED && clock() >= expiry.getValue(s)) {
            state[s] = SeatState.AVAILABLE; owner.remove(s); expiry.remove(s)
        }
    }
}

Walk-through. lockSeats(bob, [A2, A3]) while Alice holds A2: loop finds A2 is LOCKED, returns false before any write, so A3 is unchanged. confirm at minute 6: expireIfStale frees the seat, the owner check fails, IllegalStateException("lock lost"): the app should now refund the payment (see Concurrency).

Common interview traps.

  • Validating seats and mutating inside the same loop (partial lock on failure).
  • Treating > instead of >= for expiry, creating a one-millisecond window where two people own a seat.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P10 OK

The test uses a fake clock array. It asserts: Alice's hold works; Bob's overlapping request fails and A3 is not leaked; Alice's payment books both seats at 2 x 250 = 500; a hold expires after exactly 5 minutes and another user can take the seat; Bob's late payment is rejected; and 100 threads released together by a CountDownLatch all try the same seat: exactly one wins.

Common interview traps.

  • A race test that starts threads one by one never really races them. Use a latch.
  • Asserting only "no exception"; assert the number of winners.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
This is the heart of the problem: the double-booking race. Two requests read "A5 is free" at the same instant, both write "A5 is mine". The fix is making check-and-set atomic.

Options, in the order you would reach for them:

  1. synchronized per show (shown). One JVM, simple, correct. 100 racing threads produce exactly one winner. Throughput is fine: the critical section is a few map operations (microseconds), so one show can serve tens of thousands of holds per second.
  2. Per-seat ReentrantLocks acquired in sorted order (A1 before A2) to avoid deadlock when two users request overlapping seats in different orders. More parallelism, more complexity.
  3. Database atomic update: UPDATE seat SET status='LOCKED', owner=?, expires_at=now()+interval '5 min' WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (...) AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR expires_at<now()); if rows affected differs from the number of seats, roll back. Works across many app servers with no extra infrastructure; the DB row lock is the arbiter.
  4. Redis SET NX PX per seat, with a Lua script to lock multiple seats atomically; a unique constraint in the DB on (show_id, seat_id) in the final bookings table as the last safety net.
  5. Optimistic concurrency: read with a version, write WHERE version = ?, retry on failure. Cheap when conflicts are rare, wasteful on a hot show.

Payment edge case (money and seats must agree). Pay succeeds but confirm fails because the lock expired: you must refund or re-offer. Mitigate by confirming only if at least 30 s of lock remain before starting payment, extending TTL when the gateway call starts, and reconciling with gateway webhooks (idempotent confirm on paymentId).

Incident pattern. Ticket drop for a popular film: 200k users in a minute. Symptom: DB CPU at 100% on the seats table, lock wait timeouts. Fixes: a queue or waiting room to admit users gradually, Redis in front for holds, short transactions, read the seat map from a cache (accept slightly stale display; the hold call is the truth).

Decision gravity. Choosing the database unique constraint (show_id, seat_id) as the final guard is a cheap safety net you should always have, whichever locking you choose.

Everyday analogy. Two people grabbing the last seat at a cinema counter: a single clerk (the lock) serves one at a time, and the second hears "sorry, sold".

Common interview traps.

  • Locking seats one by one without ordering: user X locks A1 then wants A2; user Y locks A2 then wants A1; deadlock.
  • Relying on UI to prevent double booking.
  • Cleaning expired locks only with a cron: seats remain unavailable up to a minute after expiry. Combine lazy expiry with a sweeper.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Cancellation and refunds: BOOKED to AVAILABLE with a refund policy (time before show).
  • Dynamic pricing / coupons: Strategy on price.
  • Seat-map view: read-through cache, push updates over WebSocket or SSE so other users see seats turn grey.
  • Best-available selection: algorithm picks N adjacent seats in a row.
  • Multiple theatres and cities: shard by city or theatre; each show lives on one shard.
  • Waiting room and bot protection: rate limit by user and IP, reuse the Rate limiter (P11).
  • Notifications: ticket by email/SMS/push, reuse P8.

Common interview traps.

  • Overbooking on purpose (airlines do this) without being asked; confirm business rules first.
  • Not mentioning idempotent payment callbacks.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The core bug to prevent is check-then-act on a seat; make multi-seat hold atomic (all or nothing).
  • Hold is a lease with TTL; confirm re-checks "still locked by me" because payment is slow.
  • Lazy expiry keeps correctness independent of cleanup threads; inject a clock for tests.
  • Scale-out: DB conditional update or Redis SET NX PX for locks, plus a unique constraint (show, seat) as the final guard.
  • Order lock acquisition to avoid deadlocks; handle "paid but lost the lock" with refund and idempotent webhooks.

questions.promptHtml: Why do seats go through a hold (lock with expiry) before being booked, and why does lazy expiry matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Payment is slow and can fail; the answer shows you understand two-phase reservation and do not rely on cleanup threads for correctness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Paying takes tens of seconds and may fail, so we cannot book immediately and we cannot lock forever. A hold is a lease with a TTL (5 to 10 minutes): seats go AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED, and LOCKED returns to AVAILABLE on expiry or cancel. Lazy expiry means any operation that looks at a seat first treats an expired lock as available, so correctness never depends on a cleanup thread winning a race with a payment.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AVAILABLE --lockSeats--> LOCKED --confirm--> BOOKED
LOCKED --release/expiry--> AVAILABLE
confirm re-checks: still LOCKED and owner == me, after expireIfStale

confirm must verify "still locked by me": payment may finish at minute 6 after the lock expired and someone else took the seat. A background sweeper is only an optimisation for the seat-map display. Time comes from an injected clock so tests move time instead of sleeping five minutes. Use >= for expiry; > leaves a one-millisecond window where the lock is both held and free.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin

}
private fun expireIfStale(s: String) {

    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Booking immediately with no hold, or a hold with no expiry (seats stuck if the tab is closed).
  • Confirm without re-validating ownership and expiry.
  • Releasing someone else's lock in cancelHold.
  • Using System.currentTimeMillis() directly so expiry is untestable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the sweeper add? -> Faster UI refresh of seat maps; not needed for correctness.
  2. How long should the hold be? -> Long enough for payment, short enough for the next buyer; 5 to 10 minutes is common, and show a countdown.
  3. Can BOOKED return to AVAILABLE? -> Only via an explicit cancellation flow with refund.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "lock for 5 minutes". The senior explains the lease, the re-check at confirm, lazy expiry and clock injection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Ticketing sites show a countdown because the hold is a lease; expired holds silently return seats to the pool.

questions.promptHtml: How do you make a multi-seat hold all-or-nothing and safe against double booking? Compare a lock per show with per-seat locks, a database update, and Redis.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core of the problem is a check-then-act race; they want options with trade-offs, including deadlock avoidance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Validate every requested seat first, then mutate; nothing changes if any seat is taken, so there is no rollback. The simplest correct approach is one lock per show (synchronized), since the invariant spans seats and the critical section is microseconds. Per-seat locks give more parallelism but must be acquired in sorted order to avoid deadlock. Across servers use a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE' (check rows affected) or Redis SET NX PX, with a unique (show_id, seat_id) constraint on bookings as the final guard.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
user X wants A1,A2   user Y wants A2,A1
per-seat locks in request order: X locks A1, Y locks A2, both wait -> deadlock
fix: always lock in sorted order (A1 then A2)

Options:

  1. synchronized per show: simple, reversible; hot shows can become a bottleneck.
  2. Per-seat ReentrantLock in sorted order.
  3. DB: one UPDATE seat SET status='LOCKED', owner=?, expires_at=... WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (...) AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR expires_at < now()); if rows affected differs from the number of seats, roll back.
  4. Redis SET key NX PX 300000 per seat, with a Lua script for multi-seat atomicity.
  5. Optimistic version and retry: good when conflicts are rare, wasteful on a hot show.

    long exp = clock.getAsLong() + lockTtlMs;
    for (String s : seats) { state.put(s, SeatState.LOCKED); lockOwner.put(s, userId); lockExpiry.put(s, exp); }
    return true;
}
@Synchronized fun lockSeats(user: String, seats: List<String>): Boolean {
    seats.forEach { expireIfStale(it) }
    if (seats.any { state[it] != SeatState.AVAILABLE }) return false
    val exp = clock() + ttlMs
    seats.forEach { state[it] = SeatState.LOCKED; owner[it] = user; expiry[it] = exp }
    return true
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Validating and mutating in the same loop (partial lock on failure).
  • Locking seats in request order, causing deadlock.
  • Relying on the UI to stop double booking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the JVM lock not enough in production? -> Multiple app servers; the DB or Redis is the arbiter.
  2. What is the final safety net? -> A unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) in the bookings table.
  3. How do you test the race? -> 100 threads released by a CountDownLatch on the same seat; assert exactly one winner.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "use a lock". The senior shows all-or-nothing validation, lock ordering, the DB/Redis equivalents and the unique-constraint guard.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hot ticket drops show up as lock waits and DB CPU on the seats table; the lock choice decides where the pressure goes.

questions.contextHtml:
QA reports: "Bob tried to book A2 and A3 while Alice held A2; his request failed, but now nobody can book A3." Also seats occasionally appear double-held at exactly the expiry millisecond.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized boolean lockSeats(String user, List<String> seats) {
    long exp = clock.getAsLong() + ttl;
    for (String s : seats) {
        if (state.get(s) == SeatState.LOCKED && clock.getAsLong() > lockExpiry.get(s)) free(s);
        if (state.get(s) != SeatState.AVAILABLE) return false;
        state.put(s, SeatState.LOCKED); lockOwner.put(s, user); lockExpiry.put(s, exp);
    }
    return true;
}
@Synchronized fun lockSeats(user: String, seats: List<String>): Boolean {
    val exp = clock() + ttl
    for (s in seats) {
        if (state[s] == SeatState.LOCKED && clock() > expiry.getValue(s)) free(s)
        if (state[s] != SeatState.AVAILABLE) return false
        state[s] = SeatState.LOCKED; owner[s] = user; expiry[s] = exp
    }
    return true
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a "rollback" for A3 after failure, which is still racy and more code.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must multi-seat holds be all-or-nothing (yes)? Is the clock monotonic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Release leaked locks: seats LOCKED by a user without an active session; they will also expire after the TTL.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) validation and mutation share one loop, so A3 was locked before A2 failed; (b) > rather than >= for expiry leaves a one-millisecond ambiguity; (c) no IllegalArgumentException for unknown seats (a null from state.get).
  4. How I'd verify: Test: Alice holds A2; Bob requests A2,A3, expects false and A3 still AVAILABLE; a test at exactly the expiry millisecond.
  5. Root cause: Check and change are interleaved, so a failure part-way leaves partial state.
  6. Fix: Two passes: first validate every seat (including lazy expiry, using >=), return false if any fails; then mutate all.
  7. Prevention: Atomicity test and the latch race test; review rule: no mutation before the last check.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rollback loops. If checks pass and mutation is under the same lock, nothing to undo.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicate seats in the request (A1, A1)? -> Deduplicate or reject; sorting also helps lock ordering.
  • Empty list? -> Reject with a validation error.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Partially locked seats showed as "sold" in the map for five minutes after each failed group booking, hurting conversion until the validation pass was separated.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: does not notice the partial lock.
  • Hire: two-pass check then mutate, >=.
  • Strong hire: also tests it, validates input, and explains why rollback is unnecessary.

questions.contextHtml:
A customer is charged 500 but sees "Booking failed: lock lost". Three such tickets per 1,000 bookings. Timeline from logs:

10:00:00 hold A1,A2 user=alice ttl=300s expires 10:05:00
10:04:40 payment started (gateway p99 = 45 s)
10:05:10 payment SUCCESS webhook paymentId=P91
10:05:10 confirm -> IllegalStateException lock lost for A1
10:05:02 hold A1 user=dave  (A1 expired at 10:05:00)
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how do you design the money-and-seat consistency?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the TTL to an hour." Seats sit unsold, and the race still exists on slow payments.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the gateway be asked to cancel before capture? Do we use auth-then-capture? Is the webhook idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Auto-refund every payment whose confirm failed and email the user; reconcile today's gateway successes against bookings.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) payment started with only 20 s left on the hold; the p99 45 s exceeds it; (b) the hold expired mid-payment and another user took the seats (correct behaviour, bad flow); (c) webhook delivered late. Red herring: clock skew, since one clock decides expiry.
  4. How I'd verify: Join payment start times with lock expiries; histogram of remaining TTL at payment start.
  5. Root cause: The lease can expire while a payment is in flight; confirm then correctly rejects, but the money already moved.
  6. Fix: Require at least 60 s of remaining lock before starting payment, and extend the lock (for example +2 minutes, once) when payment starts; use authorise-then-capture and capture only after confirm succeeds; make confirm idempotent on paymentId; if confirm fails after payment, refund or re-offer similar seats; reconcile from gateway webhooks.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized boolean extend(String user, List<String> seats, long extraMs) {
    for (String s : seats) { expireIfStale(s); if (!user.equals(lockOwner.get(s))) return false; }
    for (String s : seats) lockExpiry.put(s, lockExpiry.get(s) + extraMs);
    return true;
}
@Synchronized fun extend(user: String, seats: List<String>, extraMs: Long): Boolean {
    seats.forEach { expireIfStale(it) }
    if (seats.any { owner[it] != user }) return false
    seats.forEach { expiry[it] = expiry.getValue(it) + extraMs }
    return true
}
  1. Prevention: Metric: remaining TTL at payment start, confirm-failed-after-payment count (alert above 0.05%); chaos test with a slow gateway.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Extending locks reduces availability slightly; cap extensions. Not holding seats until the webhook indefinitely.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Webhook arrives twice? -> Idempotent confirm keyed by paymentId.
  • User closes the tab mid-payment? -> The hold expires; if the payment succeeds later, refund automatically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Paid-but-failed bookings were a support headache until the team made capture conditional on a successful confirm.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only longer TTL.
  • Hire: remaining-TTL check, extension, refund.
  • Strong hire: auth/capture, idempotent webhook confirm, reconciliation and metric.

questions.contextHtml: The booking core works. Product now wants: (1) cancellation with refund rules (100% more than 24 h before the show, 50% from 24 to 2 h, none inside 2 h), (2) dynamic pricing (weekend, premium rows, coupons), and (3) a "best available N adjacent seats" button. Today Show computes price = pricePerSeat * seats.size() and has no cancel.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which patterns apply, and what must not be broken?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds if (weekend) price *= 1.2 and a cancel that just sets BOOKED to AVAILABLE.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can refunds be partial per seat? Are coupons stackable? What counts as "adjacent" across aisles? Is pricing fixed at hold time or at payment?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would ship cancellation first, since refunds are a legal and customer-trust matter.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (designs): (a) PricingStrategy (Strategy) injected into BookingService; (b) RefundPolicy computed from showTime - now with an injected clock; (c) bestAvailable(n) as a pure function over the seat map producing candidates, then the normal lockSeats.
  4. How I'd verify: Table-driven tests for refund windows at the boundaries (24:00:00 vs 23:59:59); pricing tests per row type and coupon; adjacency test with gaps.
  5. Root cause of design pressure: Price and refund rules change often and independently of seat state.
  6. Fix: Booking gets a status (CONFIRMED, CANCELLED) and the price snapshot at confirm time; cancel transitions BOOKED to AVAILABLE under the show lock and returns a refund calculated by RefundPolicy; pricing is a strategy computed once and stored on the booking. Best available proposes seats but still goes through lockSeats (the atomic check) so a stale suggestion cannot double-book.
  7. Prevention: Keep seat-state transitions in Show only; tests for each transition; audit trail of cancellations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not recomputing price at refund time with today's rules; use the snapshot. Do not skip the lock because "best available" already checked.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Refund fails at the gateway? -> Record a pending refund and retry idempotently.
  • Cancelled seat resale race? -> Same lockSeats path.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A price recomputed at refund time after a weekend surcharge change refunded the wrong amounts on 800 bookings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: inline if and a status flip.
  • Hire: Strategy for pricing and refund policy, price snapshot.
  • Strong hire: transitions only in Show, best-available reusing the atomic lock, boundary tests.

questions.contextHtml: The team has a test that books a seat with Thread.sleep(5 * 60 * 1000) to check expiry (it takes 5 minutes and is commented out) and a race test that starts 100 threads in a loop with new Thread(...).start() and asserts "no exception". It never fails even after the lock was accidentally removed from lockSeats.
questions.promptHtml: Rewrite the strategy so the tests are fast and actually catch the race.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run the test many times" or "use Thread.sleep(10) before asserting".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can Show take a clock? Is the seat state observable? How many cores does CI have?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put the lock back; find why CI passed (the test did not race).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) threads start one by one, so they rarely overlap; (b) the assertion checks no exception, not the outcome; (c) time is real.
  4. How I'd verify: Mutation check: delete synchronized from lockSeats and confirm the new test fails (more than one winner).
  5. Root cause: Test shape: no simultaneous release and no outcome assertion.
  6. Fix: Fake clock (long[] now, advance by 5 minutes), and a latch-based race:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(100);
AtomicInteger winners = new AtomicInteger();
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    String u = "u" + i;
    pool.submit(() -> { try { go.await(); if (svc.hold("S1", u, List.of("E5"))) winners.incrementAndGet(); }
                        catch (InterruptedException ignored) {} finally { done.countDown(); } });
}
go.countDown(); done.await();
assertEquals(1, winners.get());
val go = CountDownLatch(1); val done = CountDownLatch(100); val winners = AtomicInteger()
repeat(100) { i ->
    pool.submit {
        try { go.await(); if (svc.hold("S1", "u$i", listOf("E5"))) winners.incrementAndGet() }
        finally { done.countDown() }
    }
}
go.countDown(); done.await()
assertEquals(1, winners.get())

Other assertions: Bob's overlapping request fails and A3 stays free; expiry at exactly TTL; late payment rejected; two-seat requests in opposite orders from two threads do not deadlock (with a timeout). 7. Prevention: Run the race test with a repeat annotation (for example 100 iterations); add it to CI; keep it deterministic about the outcome. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No sleeps to "give threads time". Races are probabilistic, so a passing test proves less than a failing one; mutation testing the lock is the proof.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How to test the DB-level lock? -> An integration test against a real DB (testcontainers) with two connections.
  • Deadlock test? -> Two threads request overlapping seats in opposite order, join with a timeout.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A booking race test passed for a year with the lock deleted, because threads were started sequentially; a latch made it fail on the first run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sleeps and "no exception".
  • Hire: fake clock, latch race, winners assertion.
  • Strong hire: mutation check, deadlock test with timeout, DB integration test.

questions.contextHtml:
A blockbuster presale opens at 10:00 with 200,000 users in the first minute for a 600-seat show. The service uses a SQL seats table with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE per request and runs 40 app servers. At 10:00:20:

db cpu 100%   active connections 1,200/1,200   lock_wait_timeouts 31,000/min
p99 hold latency 18 s   error rate 62%
top query: SELECT * FROM seats WHERE show_id=? FOR UPDATE   (same 600 rows, held 40-300 ms)
cache hit on seat-map reads: 0% (map fetched from DB each page load)
questions.promptHtml: How do you survive this tonight, and what is the redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale the database vertically." The contention is on 600 rows, so more CPU does not help.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the show the only hot one? Can we gate admission? Is the seat map allowed to be slightly stale? What is the SLO and the acceptable error for the unlucky users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable a waiting room admitting a few hundred users per minute; serve the seat map from cache; shorten transactions; shed excess with a friendly queue page.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) FOR UPDATE over all show rows serialises everyone on the same rows; (b) seat map reads hit the DB, adding load; (c) connection pool saturated by waiting transactions. Red herring: network.
  4. How I'd verify: DB wait events and lock graphs; transaction duration histogram; connection pool metrics.
  5. Root cause: A hot-spot of 600 rows, contended by 200k users, with long pessimistic locks and reads on the same store.
  6. Fix: A waiting room/queue to cap concurrency; hold via an atomic conditional update on requested seats only (UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE' ... , check rows affected) instead of locking all rows; or Redis SET NX PX for seat holds with a Lua multi-seat script, flushing confirmed bookings to SQL with a unique (show_id, seat_id) constraint; seat-map reads from cache and pushed updates (SSE/WebSocket), accepting stale display because the hold call is the truth; rate limit per user and IP (bots).
  7. Prevention: Load test with a synthetic 200k spike; per-show circuit breaker; pre-warm cache; runbook for waiting-room switch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The waiting room reduces conversions for some users but protects the system. Redis holds add a component and a consistency boundary with SQL (the unique constraint remains the final guard). I would not scale the database first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Redis fails mid-sale? -> Fall back to DB conditional updates at lower throughput; holds in flight expire by TTL.
  • Fairness of the queue? -> Randomised admission or FIFO tokens; decide with product.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A presale melted the primary DB because every request locked the same 600 rows; a waiting room plus conditional updates cut DB load by an order of magnitude.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale vertically.
  • Hire: waiting room, atomic conditional update, cached seat map.
  • Strong hire: Redis holds with the unique-constraint guard, backpressure, bots, load test and failover.

questions.contextHtml: The booking service moves from 1 JVM (synchronized per show) to 12 stateless instances behind a load balancer. Two designs are proposed: (A) conditional SQL updates on the seats table; (B) Redis SET NX PX per seat with TTL 5 minutes, writing confirmed bookings to SQL. Expected peak: 3,000 holds/s overall, one show reaching 800/s. Redis runs as a primary with an async replica.
questions.promptHtml: Choose one, state the failure modes, and say whether the decision is a one-way door.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is faster, use Redis", without noting failover can lose a lock, or "use SQL because transactions" without the hot-row cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we tolerate a rare double hold if the final booking is guarded? Is the DB the source of truth for money? What is the failover behaviour and how often? Is cross-region needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; this is a design choice made before migration. For the migration itself keep the old JVM lock as the single writer until cutover.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): (A) SQL: strong consistency, no new component, fine at 3,000/s if transactions are short and indexed; hot show at 800/s is acceptable (row updates). (B) Redis: lower latency, offloads SQL; failure modes: async replica failover can lose a recent lock (two users hold the same seat), lock TTL vs payment time, a Lua script must handle multiple seats atomically.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test the hottest show at 2x; failover test on Redis; measure the conflict and rollback rate.
  5. Root cause of the trade-off: Consistency vs latency; the arbiter must be one place.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Start with (A): conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE' OR expires_at < now() and check rows affected, plus a unique (show_id, seat_id) constraint on bookings. Move holds to Redis only if SQL becomes the bottleneck, keeping SQL's unique constraint as the final guard so a lost Redis lock cannot become a double booking, only a failed confirmation.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
int updated = jdbc.update(
    "UPDATE seat SET status='LOCKED', owner=?, expires_at=? " +
    "WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (?,?) AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR expires_at <= ?)",
    user, exp, showId, s1, s2, now);
if (updated != 2) { tx.rollback(); return false; }
val updated = jdbc.update(
    "UPDATE seat SET status='LOCKED', owner=?, expires_at=? " +
    "WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (?,?) AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR expires_at <= ?)",
    user, exp, showId, s1, s2, now)
if (updated != 2) { tx.rollback(); return false }
  1. Prevention: The unique constraint, the metric confirm_failed_lock_lost, canary traffic, and a reconciliation job.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Choosing SQL first is a two-way door (the interface hold/confirm stays the same). Moving the source of truth later for money is the one-way door, so keep SQL authoritative from day one. I would not use Redlock style cross-node locking for money without understanding its failure assumptions (verify).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The hot show at 800/s degrades SQL? -> Shard by show (each show on one partition) and move holds for hot shows to Redis.
  • Clock differences between app servers for expires_at? -> Use the database clock (now()), not each app server's.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A Redis failover let two users hold the same seat for 30 seconds; the SQL unique constraint caught it at confirm and the team added the lock-lost metric.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks on speed alone.
  • Hire: SQL conditional update with the unique constraint, notes Redis failover risk.
  • Strong hire: staged recommendation, DB clock, hot-show sharding, reversibility analysis and reconciliation.
